source: Pease (2007) A Computational Model of Lakatos-style Reasoning (PhD thesis, Edinburgh), overview and design
finding: First full program of Lakatos's methods. HRL is a multi-agent dialogue system. Each agent runs the HR theory-formation program on its own share of the objects, so agents hold different theories. They swap conjectures, find counterexamples, then apply surrender, monster-barring, exception-barring (piecemeal exclusion, counterexample-barring, strategic withdrawal) or lemma-incorporation to change conjectures, concept definitions or proofs.
numbers: Tested in 3 domains (group theory, animal taxonomy, number theory). Default session: 10 independent work phases of 10 theory-formation steps each. Three hypotheses: each of surrender, monster-barring, exception-barring can be 'fine-tuned' by parameters.
quote: This is the first systematic automated realisation of Lakatos's theory.
limits: Pre-LLM. Concepts and conjectures are only empirical (hold on the given objects). Evaluation is by parameter sweeps and the author's own judgement of what is a 'monster' or an 'interesting' result. No statistics, no baseline.
agent_relevance: Gives a ready list of repair operators with explicit trigger conditions. Our S5 Revise could expose 4 named repairs (surrender, bar the case, add exception, add lemma) instead of one free-form 'fix it'.

source: Pease (2007) thesis ch. 9, Algorithms 8 to 10: which lemma-incorporation to perform
finding: The type of counterexample is decided by code, not judgement. Test the object against the global conjecture and each lemma of the proof. Global and local: compose the faulty lemma's concept into the premise (new conjecture C implies Q). Local only (Lakatos's cube): the conclusion still holds but the reason is wrong, so generalise the faulty lemma. Global only: a hidden lemma must be found, the hardest case, driven by 'surprise' at an object. No counterexample: return conjecture and proof unchanged.
numbers: Algorithm 8 order of tests: (1) does the global counterexample also break a lemma? (2) if not, does any lemma have a counterexample linked to it by a concept? (3) else hidden lemma-incorporation. Worked on Euler V-E+F=2 (cube, picture frame, cylinder).
quote: If there is no counterexample, then the student returns the conjecture and proof unchanged.
limits: Needs a proof scheme with machine-checkable lemmas. Hidden-lemma case is only partly implemented ('one of the most difficult methods to implement'). Toy domains.
agent_relevance: Direct answer to SUBFIELDS question (a)/(b): the 3-way type (conclusion only / premise only / both) can be computed by running the failing item against the premises and the conclusion separately. Map: premise-only hit -> fix the step; both -> restrict the claim by that premise; conclusion-only -> hunt a hidden assumption.

source: Pease (2007) thesis ch. 10.4: tuning monster-barring (sessions 1-24 and 69-92)
finding: Best rule for when to propose barring an object: bar any entity that is a counterexample to the conjecture under discussion (the 'Lakatos variable'). A minimum of 30 to 40 percent of conjectures broken also worked. Stricter 'culprit breaker' settings (object breaks more than half the theory) caught nothing useful. In number theory the system never flagged 0 or 1, because the one student set to bar never met a conjecture they broke.
numbers: 24 sessions with 1 barring student and 2 surrendering students; later sessions 69-92 with all students barring. Correct-classification score reached 97 percent in number theory only because nothing was flagged. Barring minimum tested from 0 to 100 in steps of 10.
limits: Preliminary. Score counts both monsters and non-monsters against the author's own list of monsters. Result depended on how data was split between students. No significance tests.
agent_relevance: Monster-barring (redefining the term so the case no longer counts) is the cheap, dangerous repair. Treat it as allowed only when the object also fails a stated definition check, and log it; otherwise it is the fixation trap of excluding awkward cases.

source: Pease (2007) thesis ch. 10.3: tuning surrender
finding: Best setting for number of modifications before giving up was 0: drop any conjecture as soon as a counterexample is found. Worst was 3, which modified every discussed conjecture even when students rated it uninteresting. Only the animal-taxonomy domain produced conjectures interesting enough to be worth modifying.
numbers: Interestingness threshold 0.8 (mean over all students' theories). Five surrender variables tested across 3 domains.
limits: Authors say the result mostly shows the interestingness setting is wrong; the measure is each student's own subjective score.
agent_relevance: Repair is only worth its cost if the claim is worth keeping. Add a keep-or-drop gate before S5: if the claim is cheap to regenerate and low value, resample instead of repairing.

source: Pease (2007) thesis ch. 10.5: tuning exception-barring (piecemeal exclusion, counterexample-barring, strategic withdrawal)
finding: Piecemeal exclusion worked best in group theory, which shows the system was not tuned only to number theory. Letting only some agents do counterexample-barring seemed to improve the modifications. Number theory example: 'all integers a with a|a and a*a=a' was repaired by adding 'a is not 1'.
numbers: Too few modifications per session to set optimal parameters (authors' words). Same number-theory conjectures were monster-barred (excluding 0 and 1 from the concept) in the monster-barring runs.
limits: Small counts, no significance tests. Excluding named exceptions can leave a claim with little content.
agent_relevance: Same counterexample can be handled two ways (bar it from the concept, or add it as an exception to the claim). Letting the program try both and compare retained coverage is a cleaner choice than asking the model which is better.

source: Pease (2007) thesis ch. 12 (also Colton and Pease 2004): Theorem Modifier applied to automated theorem proving
finding: Lakatos-style modification was used to rescue false or open conjectures. The Theorem Modifier takes a non-theorem, finds supporting and falsifying examples with the model finder MACE, lets HR invent specialisation concepts true of the supporting examples, then asks the prover Otter to prove the conjecture restricted to each concept. Modified statements that are proved are reported.
numbers: 98 invented non-theorems (made from TPTP theorems by removing axioms, changing quantifiers, variables or bracketing): valid modifications for 83 percent, average 3.1 modifications each. 9 non-theorems already in TPTP: 7 of 9 (78 percent). Otter and MACE 10 s each, HR 3000 steps. Example RNG031-6 (rings): proved true for rings where x*x=x implies x+x=x.
limits: 'Valid' means proved by Otter, not that it is interesting or deep. Interestingness filter is heuristic (flags trivial algebra and restatements). Small, hand-built test set.
agent_relevance: Closest old system to an automated 'add a condition so the claim becomes provable' loop. The pattern (find examples on both sides, name a class that separates them, check restricted claim by a prover) is code-checkable and fits our S5 plus S7.

source: Pease (2007) thesis ch. 13.1.1: the problem of content
finding: Every added lemma, condition or exception shrinks the domain of the theorem. Lakatos called overspecialising 'throwing the baby out with the bath water'. When a claim has been narrowed too far, the right move is surrender and a new start from the original problem.
numbers: No experiment; proposal only. Suggests tracking how specialised a conjecture has become to decide when to give up.
limits: Future-work section, not implemented.
agent_relevance: Add a coverage meter to S5: the share of the original positive examples still covered after each repair. If coverage falls below a set threshold, stop repairing and resample (surrender). Prevents the loop from ending with a trivially true claim.

source: Martin and Pease (2013) Mathematical practice, crowdsourcing, and social machines
finding: Empirical look at MathOverflow and mini-Polymath through a Lakatos lens. Counterexamples and examples were common in real mathematical talk and errors were openly corrected.
numbers: Sample of MathOverflow questions: 90 percent got a response flagged as an answer (78 percent reasonable answers, 12 percent partial). In 34 percent of responses explicit examples or counterexamples were given; 37 percent contained corrected errors; 56 percent cited literature.
quote: explicit examples were given, as evidence for, or counterexamples to, conjectures: thus playing exactly the role envisaged by Lakatos
limits: Sample size not stated in the text I read; hand coding; preliminary study. Little concept formation seen in MathOverflow, more in Polymath.
agent_relevance: Human practice: a third of useful replies are examples or counterexamples, and corrected errors are normal. Supports giving the agent a dedicated example-and-counterexample step and treating a found error as routine, not as failure.

source: Werndl (2013) Justifying Definitions in Mathematics, Going Beyond Lakatos
finding: Lakatos's proof-generated definitions (change a definition so that the proof works) are only one way to justify a definition. From a case study of randomness in ergodic theory, three others are natural-world justification, condition justification and redundancy justification, and they interact.
numbers: One case study (definitions of randomness in ergodic theory); no counts.
limits: Philosophy of mathematics, single case; says nothing about machines.
agent_relevance: Warns against making 'redefine the term until the proof works' the only concept repair. A redefinition should also pass a check against the thing the term was meant to describe, which is code-checkable when we hold examples.

source: Davis (2021) Deep Learning and Mathematical Intuition: A Review of Davies et al. (2021), knot signature case
finding: A real conjecture refinement by counterexample, with a model in the loop. Humans formed a conjecture linking knot signature to slope and volume, built a new dataset to look for counterexamples, found some, and revised the bound to include the injectivity radius. They then proved it. A critic says the neural net only did two of the steps.
numbers: Net predicted signature at 78 percent accuracy; slope alone also gave 78 percent. First hypothesis: |2 sigma - slope| < c1 vol + c2. Counterexample dataset about 36,000 knots of one category. Revised: |2 sigma - slope| < c vol / inj^3. ML used only in steps 4 and 5 of 11.
limits: Secondary review of the Nature paper, not the paper itself. Reviewer argues ordinary statistics would have found the same relation. Not an LLM.
agent_relevance: Pattern to copy: weak claim, then a targeted search for counterexamples in a region where it is most likely to fail, then add the missing variable to the claim. The counterexample search is plain code on a purpose-built dataset.

source: Chen and Jiang (2026) Lectures on AI for Mathematics, ch. 5 and knot case
finding: Lecture notes describe an LLM counterexample loop: generate a candidate, send to a verifier, get a specific error reason, regenerate with the history of failed attempts, repeat to a cap. They state that feedback quality is the key point: a bare 'incorrect' gives the generator nothing to fix. They retell the knot case: counterexamples did not end the project but pointed to a refined conjecture.
numbers: No measurements; textbook-style description.
limits: Lecture notes and secondary source. The loop description is a design recipe, not a tested result.
agent_relevance: Supports the SCHEMA rule that a revision must cite the actual failing output (G2) and that failed attempts are kept in a history list so the model does not repeat them.

source: Mining Math Conjectures from LLMs: A Pruning Approach (2024), arXiv 2412.16177
finding: GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Gemini 1.5 Flash proposed conjectures about group solubilizers and wrote GAP code to test them. A false conjecture was added to the prompt as a known failure and the loop repeated. Most outputs were duplicates and most generated code did not run. The loop only prunes; it never turns a false conjecture into a narrower true one.
numbers: 757 outputs, 420 unique (55.48 percent of 757; Gemini 237 unique, ChatGPT 94, Claude 89). Counterexample found by code: 109 (25.95 percent). No counterexample found: 40 (9.52 percent): ChatGPT 25, Gemini 11, Claude 4. Non-executable code: 271 (64.52 percent); Gemini 81.86 percent, Claude 49.44, ChatGPT 37.76 of own unique. Two code revisions allowed. Mean cosine self-similarity 0.22 to 0.42; more trials did not raise diversity.
quote: the theorem and it's result is added to the prompt, and the process is repeated with the false conjecture added to the set of ideas that are known to fail
limits: One narrow topic (solubilizer). Surviving conjectures were only tested, not proved; an expert judged novelty. Several 'no counterexample' conjectures were easy or already known. Workshop paper.
agent_relevance: Baseline of an LLM conjecture loop with counterexamples: it behaves like surrender with a memory. A repair step (restrict, add condition) is the missing piece, and executable checks fail 65 percent of the time, so the check itself needs a retry and validation path.

source: Li et al. (2026) Learning to Disprove: Formal Counterexample Generation with LLMs, arXiv 2603.19514
finding: Fine-tuned an LLM to produce counterexamples that Lean 4 verifies. Training tasks come from a symbolic mutation: take a theorem and drop one hypothesis, so the statement becomes false. Multi-reward expert iteration also rewards a proof that the dropped hypothesis is negated. The tuned model beat general LLMs and open provers on all three benchmarks.
numbers: 575K synthetic problems. Benchmark FOR-COUNTER 1,058 problems from four counterexample textbooks. Pass@1 solved counts: tuned model 222 / 213 / 174 on the three benchmarks versus strongest baseline 127 / 144 / 111 as I read the garbled table; abstract says relative gain 47 to 74 percent at pass@1. Validation pass@1 49.8 percent versus 43 percent single-reward and 14 to 25 percent for earlier provers.
limits: Rejected from ICLR 2026 (per header). Table text is garbled in my copy, so per-model numbers need re-checking. Formal Lean setting only. Benchmark authors say the existing benchmark has inaccuracies.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis-dropping is a code-made source of false claims with known counterexamples. We can build our own rule-induction test set the same way: take a verified rule, drop a condition, and the broken case is the known counterexample.

source: Zouak et al. (2026) Counterexample Generation via Per-Theorem Symbolic Verifiers (SymCE), arXiv 2610.02444
finding: A model can solve a theorem forward and still fail to disprove a close false variant (a 'falsification gap'). Supervised fine-tuning on counterexamples alone made it worse: it learned the output shape and stopped recognising true statements, even inventing witnesses for true theorems. Reinforcement learning with a code verifier as reward repaired this.
numbers: SymCE: 4,707 false undergraduate algebra and analysis conjectures, each with a Python verifier (human audit of 177 verifier decisions: 97.7 percent accurate). Qwen3-4B: counterexample success 0.30 base, 0.35 SFT, 0.50 RLVR (dense and sparse equal, n about 347 test items). Recognition of true theorems: 0.27 base, 0.00 after SFT (4 seeds, also Gemma-3-4B), 0.66 after sparse-reward RL. Dense and sparse rewards differ by 33 points on a held-out calibration probe.
limits: 4B model; algebra and analysis only; Python verifier checks witnesses but not elegance. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Strong warning: a scaffold that only asks the model to find counterexamples will make it over-refute. Always pair the refute step with a 'is the claim in fact true?' check and a code verifier, in line with G3 and G5.

source: Li et al. (2025) One Example Shown, Many Concepts Known! COUNTERMATH, ICML 2025, arXiv 2502.10454
finding: University-level benchmark where the model must judge a statement and justify it by giving or using a counterexample. Open math models were weak; strong reasoning models were far better. Fine-tuning on 1,025 counterexample-based proofs raised judgement score and slightly raised unrelated math benchmarks.
numbers: 1,216 statement-rationale pairs from 4 textbooks (human agreement between annotation stages 95.4 percent). Judgement macro-F1: open 7B models about 30; Qwen2.5-Math-72B 41.8; Deepseek-R1 80.7 per text. Fine-tuned Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct F1 41.1 vs 38.3 base (hint prompt 39.7). Out-of-domain AIME 2024: 20.0 base to 30.0 (table rows are garbled, check before use). Example-usage rates differ: some models give an example in only 18.3 to 26.5 percent of answers.
limits: Scoring partly by GPT-4o as judge (97 percent extraction accuracy, 93.5 percent agreement with humans). Gains are small. Table layout is garbled in my copy.
agent_relevance: A hint prompt telling the model to reason by example gave only about +1.4 F1. Prompting alone does not install counterexample habits; the scaffold must force the example search as a separate, executed step.

source: Sinha et al. (2025) Can Language Models Falsify? REFUTE benchmark, arXiv 2502.19414
finding: Given a problem and a subtly wrong solution, models must write a program that prints an input where the solution fails. They rarely succeed, even though the same models can often solve the problems. Knowing the correct solution barely helps. Running code in a ReAct loop helped only DeepSeek-R1 a little, but it removed invalid-input errors.
numbers: 324 Codeforces samples from 2024-2025. Best models (o3-mini high, DeepSeek-R1) solve up to 44 to 48.7 percent of the problems but find counterexamples for under 9 percent. Random-search prompting: V3 4.0, Flash 3.7, R1 4.0, o3-mini 8.3 percent; with the correct solution as oracle V3 15.1, Flash 7.7, R1 9.9. Models rarely used a randomized search on their own.
quote: counterexample creation lags significantly behind solution generation
limits: Competitive-programming bugs, verified by running code. Table in my copy is partly garbled. Models tested were early 2025 reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Refuting is harder than solving for models, and a model cannot be trusted to hunt counterexamples by thought alone. The agent should do the search in code (random and small-case enumeration) and use the model only to explain a counterexample already found.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet, ICLR 2024, arXiv 2310.01798
finding: Self-correction gains in earlier papers came from using the true answer label to decide when to stop. Without that label, asking the model to review and fix its own answer lowered accuracy.
numbers: With oracle labels, GPT-3.5 standard to oracle: GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3, CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 89.7, HotpotQA 26.0 to 29.0; GPT-4: 95.5 to 97.5, 82.0 to 85.5, 49.0 to 59.0. Without oracle, GPT-3.5 base then rounds 1 and 2: GSM8K 75.9, 75.1, 74.7; CommonSenseQA 75.8, 38.1, 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0, 25.0, 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5, 91.5, 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0, 79.5, 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0, 49.0, 43.0. GSM8K: GPT-3.5 kept its first answer 74.7 percent of the time; changes went more often from right to wrong than wrong to right.
limits: Tests 'intrinsic' self-correction on reasoning with simple prompts from earlier papers; says nothing against correction with real external feedback. Table rows are partly garbled in my copy; row assignment inferred from layout.
agent_relevance: Core support for G2: a revision needs real failing output. A counterexample is exactly such an external signal; an opinion that 'this may be wrong' is not.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location, arXiv 2311.08516
finding: Splits self-correction into finding the mistake and fixing it. Models are poor at finding the first wrong step even in clear cases, but when told the true step, backtracking fixes it well. A small trained classifier for mistake location, trained on other tasks, beat prompting a large model.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake: 5 reasoning tasks, 300 chain-of-thought traces per task from PaLM 2 (255 wrong, 45 right in the cost-limited setting; 85 percent wrong, 15 percent right elsewhere). Models tested: GPT-4-Turbo, GPT-4, GPT-3.5-Turbo, Gemini Pro, PaLM 2 Unicorn. Backtracking with oracle location improved accuracy on all 5 tasks; random locations did not. Loss on already-correct traces plateaus once classifier accuracy is about 65 percent.
limits: Traces from one model family; synthetic-style tasks (word sorting, shuffled objects, logic). Per-model accuracy table is garbled in my copy.
agent_relevance: Fits the local-versus-global idea: locating which step a counterexample breaks is the hard part, and it should be done by code (run the steps on the failing item), after which the model is good at rewriting the step.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey, arXiv 2406.01297
finding: Survey of self-correction papers up to May 2024. No prior work shows self-correction using feedback from a prompted LLM on general tasks. It works well when reliable external feedback exists (code interpreters, tools, search). Large-scale fine-tuning can enable it. A few tasks are exceptionally suited to it. The bottleneck is generating good feedback.
numbers: Qualitative; survey. Offers a checklist for designing fair self-correction experiments.
limits: I read the abstract, introduction and section structure, not every cited result. Survey cut-off May 2024.
agent_relevance: Three-line rule for the schema: self-critique by the model alone is not evidence; counterexamples from tools are. Decide first what the external feedback is, then build the repair step around it.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning, arXiv 2303.11366
finding: After a failed attempt the agent writes a short verbal reflection, stores it in memory, and tries again. Feedback comes from tests, an environment or a heuristic. Gains were large in code and decision tasks.
numbers: HumanEval (Python) pass@1 91 percent versus GPT-4 baseline 80 percent. Reported gains over baselines: +22 percent AlfWorld, +20 percent HotPotQA, +11 percent on HumanEval (as stated in the text).
limits: Huang et al. 2024 note that some runs used ground-truth correctness to stop the loop. Gains on code rely on the model's own generated unit tests; I read the abstract, headline tables and discussion only.
agent_relevance: Memory of failed attempts plus a reflection is a cheap way to carry the history of counterexamples between rounds. Keep the reflection tied to the failing test output, as G2 requires.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug, ICLR 2024, arXiv 2304.05128
finding: Model debugs its own code using execution results or its own explanation of the code (rubber-duck style). Real unit-test feedback gave the biggest gain; explanation alone gave small gains.
numbers: Code explanation without tests: +2 to 3 percent baseline; +9 percent on hardest SQL (Spider). With unit tests (TransCoder, MBPP): up to +12 percent. Also improves sample efficiency by reusing failed predictions.
limits: Gains largest where executable tests exist. Code, not conjectures. Read abstract and intro only.
agent_relevance: Same message as Reflexion: the gain comes from running something and showing the model the output. Order of value: tests, then explanation, then plain 'check again'.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal Yet Puzzling: Testing Inductive Reasoning of LMs with Hypothesis Refinement, ICLR 2024, arXiv 2310.08559
finding: Propose, test and refine text rules on four rule-induction tasks. Refinement with a symbolic interpreter that applies the rule lifted scores a lot. Models propose good rules but cannot apply their own rules. When refining they mostly add exceptions for the failing example instead of rethinking the rule, so a wrong first guess is rarely escaped.
numbers: GPT-4. Raw accuracy, plain input-output vs refinement T=3, N=5: ACRE 64.0 to 82.5; MiniSCAN 61.7 to about 86.6; List Functions 65.1 vs about 62.4 (no gain); MiniARC 33.1 vs 18.7 (worse). Task accuracy ACRE 28.0 to 59.0; MiniSCAN 0.0 to 46.0 (T=3,N=1) and about 70.0 (T=3,N=5). Self-refine (T=3,N=5) beats plain only on ACRE (64.0 to 70.0). Noise: 12.5, 25, 50 percent of 8 exemplars perturbed on List Functions; even one noisy example hurt clearly. When the model applies its own rules, task accuracy fell from over 80 percent to near zero on MiniSCAN.
quote: adding exceptions for a specific example, rather than starting from entirely new hypotheses
limits: Four small synthetic tasks, GPT-4 era. Table layout is garbled in my copy; MiniSCAN and List Functions refinement figures are inferred from layout and should be re-checked before quoting.
agent_relevance: The best machine evidence for exception-barring as the default repair: models add 'unless' clauses. Our loop should count how often a rule gains exceptions and, at a set count, force a fresh rule (surrender) instead of a further patch.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Hypothesis Search: Inductive Reasoning with Language Models, ICLR 2024, arXiv 2309.05660
finding: GPT-4 writes many natural-language hypotheses, then turns each into a Python program that is run on the examples. Filtering hypotheses (LLM summary or human choice) and executing code both help. Execution feedback over rounds gave steady small gains.
numbers: Random 100-problem ARC subset: direct prompting 17 percent; LLM-summarised hypotheses 30 percent; human-selected from LLM candidates 33 percent; human-written hypotheses 23 percent without summary; hypotheses written but not turned into programs 19 percent. 64 candidate hypotheses summarised to 8; a correct hypothesis existed for 49 tasks, 33 (67 percent) of them led to correct programs; 28 of the 30 tasks solved had a correct hypothesis before summarising. Feedback rounds 0 to 3: 24, 28, 28, 30 percent. SyGuS 94.3 percent; 1D-ARC program-only variant 61.1 percent (table).
limits: ARC top-1 accuracy on a 100-item subset; one model. Summaries often vague and sometimes drop the correct hypothesis.
agent_relevance: Fits our ARC control: a hypothesis list plus code execution beats one-shot, and most gain is in the first feedback round. Cap refinement rounds at about 3.

source: Onda et al. (2025) LeanConjecturer: Automatic Generation of Mathematical Conjectures for Theorem Proving, arXiv 2506.22005
finding: An LLM writes Lean 4 conjectures from seed Mathlib files, a program filters out those that fail to compile, are trivially proved by aesop, or duplicate known results, and the loop repeats until no new ones appear. The conjectures were then used for reinforcement learning. Proof counts rose a lot but the number of solved problems rose only slightly.
numbers: 12,289 conjectures from 40 seed files; 3,776 valid and non-trivial (103.25 per file on average, per abstract). 15 iterations maximum; 25 of 40 files hit that cap. GRPO on DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B: proof successes 2,285 to 3,657 of 24,576 (10 epochs, about 16 hours on 8 A100); problems solved 47 to 49 of 192 (to 50 with extra semi-open set conjectures; 2,285 to 5,307 proofs overall). Context choice mattered: feeding all prior conjectures gave more varied output.
limits: Conjecture 'quality' is judged by being non-trivial and compiling, not by truth or interest. Gains do not transfer well beyond the training area. Some non-trivial conjectures are false.
agent_relevance: Conjecture generators keep producing near-copies unless the context is controlled. Cheap code filters (compile, trivial, duplicate) do most of the quality work; that is the same G5 principle.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Lyra: Orchestrating Dual Correction in Automated Theorem Proving, arXiv 2309.15806
finding: Uses 'conjecture correction' to mean feeding the prover's error message back to GPT-4 to repair a failed formal proof sketch (not a Lakatos repair of a claim). With tool correction (replace failing steps by automatic tactics) it set new miniF2F records for Isabelle. Conjecture correction helped, but needed more attempts.
numbers: miniF2F-Isabelle with GPT-4, 200 attempts: valid 55.3 percent (prior best 48.0) and test 51.2 percent (prior best 45.5); +5.7 points absolute on test. Correction rounds inserted every K=5 attempts: 200 attempts become 40 patches of 5 (1 first proof + 4 refined). Ablation shows tool correction helped consistently.
limits: The term 'conjecture' is misleading: what is corrected is a proof, not a statement. Only 488 problems; gain depends on spending 100 to 200 attempts.
agent_relevance: Naming caution for our schema: do not call error-message repair of a proof a Lakatos move. The measured part (one first try, then four error-driven repairs per batch) is a usable budget pattern for S5.

source: Ke et al. (2026) Towards Solving the Gilbert-Pollak Conjecture via LLMs, arXiv 2601.22365
finding: Instead of asking the model for the proof, they ask it for small geometric lemmas as executable code. A program assembles them into verification functions that give certified bounds. A reflection step reports which region of the search space failed and the lemmas are refined. This produced a new certified bound on the Steiner ratio; without the reflection step there was no improvement.
numbers: Lower bound on the Steiner ratio raised to 0.8559 from 0.824 (stalled for about three decades). Only thousands of LLM calls. Ablation: with bottleneck reflection removed, no improvement over 10 rounds. Result robust to the choice of LLM backbone.
limits: One problem (certified lower bound, not a proof of the conjecture). Lemma discovery is covered by a parallel subfield; here it counts as proof-generated lemmas driven by verifier failure.
agent_relevance: Best recent example of 'incorporate a lemma from where the check failed': structured feedback (which region, which lemma) beat a scalar reward. Use structured failure reports, not 'try again'.

source: Pastorek (2026) AutoGraphForge: Towards Automated Graph Theory Discovery, arXiv 2609.03478
finding: A conjecture-refute loop with no LLM in the first stages. A generator (Graffiti3) proposes inequalities over a small table of graphs. Counterexamples from a 348,207-graph test set and search algorithms are added to that small table, which grows only by counterexamples, and generation runs again until a round adds no counterexample. Survivors go to Lean and neural provers (stage still running).
numbers: Single-pass baseline: 3,959 candidates, 1,249 refuted (865 by extremal families, 217 by random graphs, 161 by House of Graphs). Five partitions of 9 targets each: round 1 added 494 to 793 counterexamples to the table of 2,860 graphs (20 to 28 percent growth); round 2 added 39 to 164; round 3 about 3 to 21; four partitions stopped at round 5, one at round 9. Search algorithms added only 1 to 22 per round. 8,281 raw survivors, merged to 6,522 (2,677 class-conditioned inequalities and 3,845 sufficient conditions). Budget 1.22 CPU-years.
limits: Ongoing project, no proofs yet, novelty only vs. 559 known relations. A conjecture surviving test graphs is not true. The dataset beat the clever searchers in this run (default settings).
agent_relevance: Shows what a Lakatos-style loop looks like at scale: yields drop fast after round 1, and the loop stops at a fixed point (no new counterexample). Use 'a round that adds nothing' as the stop signal, and cheap fixed test sets before costly search.

source: Davila (2024) The Optimist: Towards Fully Automated Graph Theory Research, arXiv 2411.09158
finding: An agent that proposes graph-theory conjectures with integer programming and heuristics and refines them as new data arrive. A counter-agent, the Pessimist, that hunts counterexamples is described as planned work. The paper notes older Graffiti systems were limited by missing small special graphs that would have been counterexamples.
numbers: No benchmark numbers in the parts I read; it reports rediscovered and new conjectures qualitatively.
limits: Pessimist not built in this paper. Qualitative. Not an LLM.
agent_relevance: Design echo of Pease's two-agent dialogue: one proposer, one refuter, split by role. A split like this would lower the correlated errors in G4 if the refuter is a code searcher, not a second sample of the same model.

source: Dong and Ma (2025) STP: Self-play LLM Theorem Provers with Iterative Conjecturing and Proving, ICML 2025, arXiv 2502.00212
finding: One model plays conjecturer and prover. The conjecturer is trained on conjectures the current prover can only barely prove, so difficulty rises. This avoids the stall of expert iteration when correct proofs are scarce.
numbers: arXiv v2 abstract: 26.3 percent of LeanWorkbook statements proved with 19.8B tokens versus 13.2 percent for earlier expert iteration; miniF2F-test 61.1 percent at pass@3200. Published ICML version reported 28.5 percent (51.3B tokens) vs 13.1 percent and miniF2F-test 65.0 percent (values from search summary, not rechecked in full text).
limits: Training method (needs weights); we do not train. The ICML numbers differ from the arXiv v2 numbers, so cite with version. Conjectures are variants of seed theorems, not repairs of failed claims. Numbers come from a search summary of the abstract, not checked against the full text this session.
agent_relevance: Idea that transfers without training: keep claims whose test result is borderline (barely passes) as the most informative ones to probe next.

source: Su et al. (2026) CIll: CTI-Guided Invariant Generation via LLMs for Model Checking, arXiv 2602.23389
finding: Loop for proving hardware properties. A model proposes helper invariants. A bounded check that finds a violation returns a counterexample to revise. If the invariants are not inductive, counterexamples to induction (CTIs) are passed to the model, which must propose a new invariant that rules the CTI out. This is the classical 'strengthen the lemma until the proof goes through' step (hidden lemma-incorporation) with an LLM as proposer.
numbers: 222 instances from RISC-V cores; baseline model checkers solved 146, leaving 76 for CIll. CIll solved all remaining PicoRV32 and NERV cases except the M extension (32-bit multiply, bit-blasting too hard), and did not solve the serv core. Attempts per solved case ranged 1 to 6 in the table; k=3 for induction checks, 15 s correctness check per round.
limits: Hardware verification; model plus IC3 engine do the hard parts. Total solved count for the 76 not stated in the lines I read.
agent_relevance: Concrete working version of 'counterexample to the proof step, not to the claim, gives the missing lemma'. The program extracts the CTI and the model's only job is to name an invariant that excludes it, then code rechecks.

source: Huang et al. (2025) Automated Hypothesis Validation with Agentic Sequential Falsifications (POPPER), ICML 2025, arXiv 2502.09858
finding: LLM agents design and run falsification experiments on a free-form hypothesis and combine p-values as e-values in a sequential test, so error stays controlled. Common LLM agents (CodeGen, ReAct) did not control false positives.
numbers: Type-I error held at 0.1 across 6 domains while ReAct and CodeGen baselines failed; on DiscoveryBench power was 66.5 percent greater than ReAct; matched human scientists in an expert study while taking about 10 times less time (5 independent runs).
limits: Tests hypotheses by data analysis, not mathematical proof; no repair step: a falsified hypothesis is simply rejected. Cites Lakatos only in the reference list.
agent_relevance: Gives a rule for when many weak checks add up to evidence without fooling ourselves. A way to treat 'passes all counterexample tests so far' as a measured claim, not a proof (G3).

source: An et al. (2026) QED: Open-Source Multi-Agent System for Generating Mathematical Proofs on Open Problems, arXiv 2604.24021
finding: Listing seven failure modes of coding agents on research proofs, including one that is a quiet monster-barring: models alter the problem statement to make it easier. The fix was a word-by-word statement-integrity check. Other fixes: separate prover and verifier contexts, a stable plan separated from execution, and structured verification in two stages.
numbers: 18 research-level projects; 5 original works judged solid by experts, 3 comparable to specialist-journal papers. Ablations were qualitative and only on 2 cases (decomposition mode produced 20-page and 15-page appendices that preserved the plan).
quote: Problem modification: Models alter the problem statement to reduce difficulty
limits: No success rates per intervention; expert judgement; ablations limited to two cases. Preprint.
agent_relevance: The LLM-side version of monster-barring and exception-barring is silently weakening the claim. Add a code check that the final claim is the same as, or stated as a strict restriction of, the original, and log every change.
